subject: history

moments.title: Fort Sumter
moments.body: 12 April 1861: Confederate batteries fire on Fort Sumter in Charleston harbour. By the end of May, eleven slave states have seceded. Lincoln calls for 75,000 volunteers. Both sides expect a short war.
moments.takeaway: Lincoln's position: secession is illegal; slavery's extension is the issue; preserving the Union is the goal. Emancipation as a war aim came later.

moments.title: Emancipation Proclamation
moments.body: 1 January 1863: the Emancipation Proclamation frees enslaved people in Confederate-controlled territory. It is a war measure under Lincoln's executive authority, not a general abolition. It changes the war from a constitutional struggle into a war of liberation.

quote.text: With malice toward none, with charity for all.

moments.takeaway: The Thirteenth Amendment (December 1865) abolished slavery throughout the United States. About 4 million enslaved people were freed.

moments.title: Appomattox and assassination
moments.body: 9 April 1865: Lee surrenders to Grant at Appomattox Court House. 14 April: Lincoln is shot at Ford's Theatre; he dies the next morning. Andrew Johnson succeeds. The war had killed around 750,000 — more Americans than all other US wars combined until Vietnam.
moments.takeaway: Reconstruction (1865-1877) attempted to remake the South. White supremacist violence and Northern political fatigue ended it in compromise.

now.title: The war's unresolved questions
now.body: Reconstruction's collapse opened the era of Jim Crow segregation (1880s-1960s). The Civil Rights Movement of the 1950s-60s was the second Reconstruction. The Confederate flag, monuments and 'Lost Cause' narratives have been contested intensely since 2015 (Charleston shooting) and 2020 (George Floyd protests).
now.open_questions: Was the Civil War inevitable? The 1850s compromises (Compromise of 1850, Kansas-Nebraska Act 1854, Dred Scott 1857) had failed in succession. Most modern scholarship (James McPherson, Eric Foner) treats slavery's expansion as the fundamental issue.

reflection: The American Civil War ended slavery and reshaped the federal state. Its memory and meaning remain contested. The questions it didn't settle — about race, federal authority, regional identity — continue to shape American politics in the 21st century.
